paper_title: HiUni: Harmonizing Understanding and Generation in Shared Visual Space

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HiUni, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HiUni introduces a \emph{Pixel Diffusion Head} tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight \emph{HiGate} pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HiUni achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HIUNI, which revisits this design choice and explores whether pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HIUNI reuses the same languagealigned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HIUNI introduces Pixel Diffusion Head tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and lightweight HiGate pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HIUNI achieves similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Image understanding translates visual content into language, whereas visual generation synthesizes images from textual descriptions. An ideal unified multimodal model (UMM) is expected to support both capabilities within single framework and facilitate cross-task interaction between them (Kang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). However, most existing UMMs still maintain two separate visual representation spaces with dedicated encoders. The understanding branch extracts high-level semantics via language-aligned Vision Transformer (ViT), while the generation branch learns fine-grained spatial details with Variational Autoencoder (VAE). As highlighted by Janus (Wu et al., 2025b), forcing two divergent encoding objectives into one representation triggers severe task interference. Bagel (Deng et al., 2025) further introduces Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture that separates task-specific computation within the backbone, establishing modular paradigm adopted by recent studies (Agarwal et al., 2026; Diao et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026). Although this separation preserves individual performance, it limits direct interaction through shared visual representations. Recent studies further suggest that closer sharing of visual representations can promote stronger interaction between the two capabilities with an appropriate backbone design (Zheng et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026). These observations motivate us to revisit whether such architectural separation is indeed necessary: Can shared visual space internally harmonize understanding and generation without relying on task-specific backbone computation? Recent advances offer promising opportunities to address this question using single visual encoder for both understanding and generation (Liu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a). Conventional generation models heavily rely on VAE latents, yet these features are optimized primarily for reconstruction and are less aligned with the high-level semantics required for understanding (Wu et al., 2025e; Ma et al., 2026a). Conversely, modern pixel-space diffusion models demonstrate that high-quality generation can also be achieved without VAE latents (Li & He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026), opening new

sections.content: Figure 1: Comparison of representative UMM designs. (a) Bagel utilizes separate visual encoders and task-specific MoT modules for understanding and generation. (b) TUNA constructs shared visual representation by cascading VAE and ViT. (c) HIUNI reuses the pretrained VLM visual pathway, while HiGate supplies fine-grained pixel details only to the generation head. path towards shared visual representations. Going one step further, some encoder-free architectures process raw pixels for both understanding and generation (Liu et al., 2026a; Diao et al., 2026), but the absence of pretrained visual semantic priors makes optimization substantially less stable and less data efficient. An alternative choice is to reuse language-aligned ViT as the shared visual encoder, given its strong semantic representations and direct compatibility with standard Vision Language Model (VLM) infrastructures. Nevertheless, adapting such an architecture to image generation introduces spatial bottleneck. VLMs typically employ patch merger after ViT to compress visual tokens, doubling effective patch size from 14/16 to 28/32 (Bai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Such aggressive spatial pooling, together with the semantic abstraction of deep ViT layers, improves understanding efficiency, but weakens fine-grained information needed for high-fidelity synthesis. Following this direction, we introduce HIUNI, UMM initialized from pretrained VLM that extends image understanding to generation through shared semantic visual pathway. Understanding and generation use the same visual encoder, token representation, and dense backbone. Task-specific computation is confined to the output modules. For image generation, we observe optimization instability when applying standard DiT to pixel-space diffusion in our early experiments. We therefore design dedicated Pixel Diffusion Head with simplified modulation for pixel-space generation. To compensate for spatial information weakened by patch merging and deep semantic abstraction, we incorporate lightweight gating module (HiGate), inspired by Cheers (Zhang et al., 2026b), which directly routes uncompressed pixel-level features to the pixel diffusion head. This residual pathway supplies local spatial cues for image generation while leaving semantic modeling in the shared visual encoder and backbone. We comprehensively validate HIUNI on image understanding, image generation, and image editing. HIUNI retains strong visual understanding capabilities inherited from the pretrained VLM while incorporating image generation into the shared backbone. It also achieves the highest overall Chinese score on Qwen-Image-Bench among the compared UMMs, together with competitive image editing performance. More importantly, further architectural comparison reveals the trade-offs between shared and task-specific backbone computation. While task-routed MoT improves generation over same-scale dense backbone under matched training settings, larger shared dense backbone with comparable total parameter count achieves substantially stronger understanding while maintaining competitive generation. These results suggest that scaling shared dense backbone within shared visual space offers simple and promising path toward unified multimodal modeling. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose HIUNI, which provides new perspective on building UMMs from pretrained VLMs. Understanding, generation, and editing share the same language-aligned encoder and dense backbone, while task-specific computation is limited to the output module. We develop Pixel Diffusion Head tailored to direct pixel-space generation, together with lightweight HiGate pathway that complements the shared semantic representation with fine-grained spatial details. Extensive experiments show that HIUNI maintains strong understanding while achieving competitive generation and editing performance. Controlled comparisons further highlight that shared dense backbone has the potential to effectively support both understanding and generation without task-specific backbone computation.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Unified Multimodal Models. UMMs are intended to support visual understanding and generation within single model. Existing UMMs mainly follow two paradigms according to how images are represented and generated. Autoregressive models tokenize images into discrete visual tokens and model text and vision under unified autoregressive objective (Team, 2024; Cui et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025e; Team et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). This formulation provides simple and scalable interface across modalities, but discrete tokenization may lose subtle visual details required for high fidelity image synthesis. Another line of work follows the Transfusion paradigm (Zhou et al., 2025), which retains the autoregressive prediction of language while applying diffusion or flow matching to continuous visual features for image generation (Deng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b; Yan et al., 2026). More recently, pixel-space diffusion further demonstrates that strong image synthesis can be achieved without VAE latents (Li & He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026), and local details can be recovered from noisy pixels to complement global semantic modeling (Chen et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026b), opening more direct path toward shared visual representations. Together, these advances shift an important architectural question toward how visual representations and backbone computation should be shared between understanding and generation. Visual Unification. The architectural design of UMMs depends on how visual representations and backbone computation are organized. Many existing models maintain separate visual spaces due to the different requirements of understanding and generation, where language-aligned ViT provides semantic features for understanding, and reconstruction-oriented VAE preserves fine-grained details for generation (Wu et al., 2025b; Deng et al., 2025). To reduce this separation, recent studies explore more unified visual pathways. TUNA cascades VAE encoder with representation encoder to construct shared visual representation, while TUNA-2 further removes both encoders for pixel space modeling (Liu et al., 2026b;a). Cheers decouples semantic representations and local details through unified visual tokenizer and gated detail residuals in generation head (Zhang et al., 2026b). HYDRA adopts progressive ViT, and UniSpace introduces reconstruction aware patch representations into pretrained ViT (Zhang et al., 2026a; Yan et al., 2026). These designs reduce visual separation, but differ in their use of pretrained visual encoders and task-specific backbone computation. For example, UniSpace still adopts task-specific Transformer experts, while encoder-free models such as SenseNova remove both ViT and VAE but retain an MoT backbone (Yan et al., 2026; Diao et al., 2026). In another related direction, RepFusion processes noisy visual representations through pretrained VLM, but relies on separate diffusion Transformer for representation-space generation (Pan et al., 2026). HIUNI reuses the ViT and patch merger of pretrained VLM and shares their output representation and single dense backbone across understanding and generation, without separate generative visual encoders or task-specific backbone computation.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: Image understanding and generation differ substantially in their input and output forms, but both rely on semantic alignment between visual content and language. HIUNI therefore separates shared semantic modeling from task-specific prediction. Specifically, we seek to let the visual encoder and multimodal backbone provide common semantic pathway for both capabilities, while introducing generation-specific processing only when detailed visual signals need to be reconstructed. This design allows understanding and generation to share the visual and backbone computation without requiring separate semantic representations. Following this principle, HIUNI is built upon pretrained VLM and extends it with image generation capability while reusing its pretrained visual encoder and backbone architecture. Both understanding and generation use the same language-aligned ViT, the same visual tokens after patch merging, and the same dense backbone. Textual outputs are predicted by the native language modeling head, while image synthesis is handled by new Pixel Diffusion Head. No separate semantic visual encoder or task-specific backbone is involved. To compensate for the spatial information weakened by patch merging and deep semantic abstraction, HIUNI further adopts lightweight gating module, termed HiGate, which routes raw features from the noisy image to the diffusion head. The residual branch supplies local spatial cues to complement the shared semantic representation without modifying the main semantic computation. Figure 2 illustrates the overall architecture.

sections.title: 3.1 UNIFIED MULTIMODAL ARCHITECTURE
sections.content: Shared Visual Encoding. HIUNI adopts language aligned ViT from the pretrained VLM as the only visual encoder for both understanding and generation. Let denote the ViT and denote the patch merger, which compresses the ViT outputs into visual tokens. For an input image x, the visual tokens are obtained as = M(E(x)). The same pathway is used for clean images in understanding and visual conditioning, as well as noisy target images in generation. Consequently, both tasks are grounded in the same visual token space without requiring separate or task-specific encoders. Shared Dense Backbone. The shared visual tokens are further processed by the same dense backbone for both understanding and generation. Text embeddings and visual tokens are organized into multimodal sequence and processed by single dense Transformer B, yielding = B(S). Attention mask allows bidirectional interaction within each image, while text tokens retain causal attention for autoregressive prediction. After the shared backbone, task-specific prediction is handled on the output side. For image understanding, the language modeling head projects hidden states corresponding to textual outputs onto the vocabulary space. For image generation, hidden states at the target visual positions are passed to the pixel diffusion head for image prediction.

sections.title: 3.2 PIXEL-SPACE IMAGE GENERATION
sections.content: Pixel Diffusion Head. Diffusion directly in pixel space poses additional optimization challenges compared with conventional latent diffusion, as the model must predict high dimensional pixel signals while maintaining semantic consistency and fine spatial structure (Jiang et al., 2026; Li & He, 2026). Consistent with these observations, we observe frequent loss spikes when using standard DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) with repeated AdaLN modulation in our early experiments. In subsequent development runs, simplified design without block-wise AdaLN exhibits smoother training trajectories. Motivated by this observation, we remove AdaLN from the DiT blocks, reducing the diffusion head to standard Transformer architecture. Timestep conditioning enters through an explicit time token and final modulation layer. Inspired by recent works (Ma et al., 2025; Team, 2025), for timestep t, sinusoidal encoding ϕ(t) is mapped by two layer MLP to time embedding et RDb , where Db denotes the hidden dimension of the backbone. The resulting vector replaces the embedding of the <time> token and is processed together with the multimodal sequence by the shared backbone. The backbone hidden states for the target visual positions, together with the time token representation, are projected to the diffusion hidden dimension and processed by Transformer blocks.

Although the unified visual tokens carry strong semantics, the patch merger reduces their spatial resolution, while deeper ViT layers increasingly favor abstraction over local texture. Such compression is well suited to understanding but may discard cues important for pixel-level reconstruction. sections.title: 3.3 TASK FORMULATION AND JOINT TRAINING
sections.content: Unified Task Formulation. HIUNI supports text-to-image generation and image editing through the same generation pathway, with the two tasks differing only in their conditioning context. For image generation, the condition is textual prompt p. For image editing, the condition consists of an editing instruction and reference image xr. The reference image follows the same visual encoding pathway as the target image and is processed together with the noisy target image by the shared backbone. Formally, we denote the conditioning context by Cτ , where τ {t2i, edit}, Ct2i = p, and Cedit = (p, xr). Given Cτ and the noisy target image xt, both tasks follow the same generation pathway without introducing task specific branches. Joint Training Objectives. HIUNI jointly optimizes language modeling, image understanding and image generation within the same backbone. Textual outputs for language modeling and image understanding are trained with the standard next token prediction objective. Let denote the input context, the language modeling objective is Ltxt = 1 i=1 log pθ(yiC, y<i). For image generation, we follow JiT (Li & He, 2026) and adopt x-prediction with velocity-based objective. The noisy image is constructed as xt = tx0 + (1 t)ϵNg . The model takes xt, timestep t, and task condition Cτ as input and directly predicts the clean image as ˆx0 = fθ(xt, t, Cτ ). sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate HIUNI on image understanding, image generation, and image editing, and further examine architectural design through controlled comparisons. Additional training and evaluation details, analyses of pixel diffusion optimization stability and cross task interaction, an extension to chain of thought image generation, and qualitative results are provided in Appendices A-F.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Implementation Details. We initialize HIUNI from Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), reusing its language model backbone as the shared dense backbone and its language aligned ViT as the shared visual encoder. The multimodal training corpus covers image understanding, image generation, and image editing, with their category distributions summarized in Figure 3. Following the three-stage procedure in Section 3.3, we first warm up the Pixel Diffusion Head and HiGate for 30K steps on image generation data while freezing all pretrained components. We then unfreeze the full model and perform 310K steps of joint pretraining on pure text modeling, image understanding, and image generation, with the generation resolution progressively increased from 256 256 to 2048 2048. Finally, we conduct 22K steps of supervised fine tuning, where image editing is added while the existing tasks are retained. The learning rate is 1 104 during generation warmup and early joint pretraining, and is reduced to 2 105 in later pretraining, while supervised fine tuning uses peak learning rate of 2 105. The complete phase-wise recipe, including training steps, batch sizes, learning rate schedules, image resolutions, loss weights, and task sampling ratios, is provided in Appendix and Table 6. Baselines. We compare HIUNI with broad set of UMMs and specialized models. Representative UMM baselines include Harmon (Wu et al., 2025d), Cheers (Zhang et al., 2026b), InternVL-U (Tian et al., 2026), Janus-Pro (Chen et al., 2025), Show-o2 (Xie et al., 2026b), TUNA (Liu et al., 2026b), Bagel (Deng et al., 2025), SenseNova-U1 (Diao et al., 2026), UniSpace (Yan et al., 2026) among others. For image understanding, we also report Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), from which HIUNI is initialized, as reference for the image understanding capability of the pretrained VLM. For image generation, we further compare against strong baselines such as GLM-Image (GLMImage Team, 2026), Qwen-Image (Wu et al., 2025a), and HiDream-O1 (Cai et al., 2026). sections.title: 4.2 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: Image Understanding. We evaluate HIUNI on eight representative benchmarks, including MathVista (Lu et al., 2024), MMBench (Liu et al., 2024a), RealWorldQA (AI, 2024), MMStar (Chen et al., 2024), HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024), AI2D (Kembhavi et al., 2016), OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024b), and OmniDocBench (Ouyang et al., 2025). As shown in Table 1, HIUNI achieves strong performance across the evaluated understanding benchmarks. Across the seven higher-isbetter benchmarks, HIUNI achieves an average score of 75.56, close to the officially reported 75.61 of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, while maintaining the same OmniDocBench score of 0.24. Compared with the re-evaluated Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking baseline under the same evaluation settings, HIUNI achieves better results on four of eight benchmarks. Performance changes are benchmark dependent, with improvements on benchmarks such as MathVista and HallusionBench and declines on others such as MMBench and OCRBench. Despite its relatively compact model scale, HIUNI achieves understanding performance comparable to several substantially larger UMMs across the evaluated benchmarks. Overall, these results indicate that strong understanding performance can coexist with image generation in the proposed shared architecture. Image Generation. We evaluate HIUNI on Qwen-Image-Bench (Li et al., 2026), OneIG (Chang et al., 2026), and LongText (Geng et al., 2025). These benchmarks provide complementary evaluations that cover perceptual quality, aesthetics, semantic alignment, realism, creativity, and the ability to render long text within images. From Table 2, we can observe that HIUNI achieves the highest Chinese score among UMMs on Qwen-Image-Bench, while remaining competitive on the English split. For OneIG and LongText, HIUNI also stays close to the strongest unified baselines, indicating strong performance on both general image generation and long text rendering. Together, these results show that HIUNI achieves strong generation capability within UMM architecture.

For GEdit (Liu et al., 2025), we follow the VIEScore protocol (Ku et al., 2024) but replace the judge backbone with GPT-5.2, which scores semantic consistency (G SC) and perceptual quality (G PQ) on scale 0 to 10. As shown in Table 3, HIUNI reaches an Overall score of 3.66 on ImgEdit, ranking second among the compared unified models behind UniSpace (3.82) and slightly ahead of SenseNova-U1 (3.65), despite its relatively compact model scale. Editing-only models that are trained exclusively for this task remain ahead, reaching 4.02 and 4.01 with LongCat-Image-Edit and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, respectively. These results further indicate the effectiveness of our unified architectural design across diverse and complex tasks.

sections.title: 4.3 TRADE-OFFS BETWEEN SHARED AND TASK-SPECIFIC COMPUTATION
sections.content: Experimental Configurations. In this section, we examine whether understanding and generation can be effectively supported by shared dense backbone. We compare three configurations, HIUNIDense-2B, HIUNI-MoT-2B, and HIUNI-Dense-4B. HIUNI-Dense-2B and HIUNI-MoT-2B are both initialized from Qwen3-VL-2B. For HIUNI-MoT-2B, the pretrained backbone is duplicated to initialize separate understanding and generation branches. These two models follow the same training recipe and differ only in whether the backbone is shared or task-routed, which both undergo 30K warmup steps followed by 30K pretraining steps. Moreover, HIUNI-Dense-4B is initialized from Qwen3-VL-4B and is included as an additional reference for allocating similar total parameter budget to larger shared backbone. We further introduce two single-task baselines, HIUNI-Und-4B and HIUNI-Gen-4B, which share the same architecture and Qwen3-VL-4B initialization as HIUNIDense-4B, but are trained exclusively on understanding and generation data, respectively, with the same training steps. For fair comparison, we adopt the same 0.5B diffusion head across all configurations, with its hidden dimension aligned to the 2B backbone. Results and Analysis. As shown in Table 4, compared with HIUNI-MoT-2B, HIUNI-Dense-2B achieves comparable understanding performance (58.55 vs. 59.23) with fully shared backbone, while its OneIG score decreases from 0.345 to 0.291. This comparison suggests that task-specific backbone computation benefits image generation under the same training settings, although shared dense backbone can also support both capabilities. Under similar total parameter budget, HIUNI-Dense-4B outperforms HIUNI-MoT-2B on all six understanding benchmarks, while retaining competitive generation performance. Notably, the shared design allows HIUNI-Dense-4B to inherit stronger pretrained representations from Qwen3-VL-4B, whereas HIUNI-MoT-2B has to distribute its capacity across two branches initialized from Qwen3-VL-2B. Within the dense architecture, scaling from 2B to 4B improves the understanding average by 11.1% and the OneIG score by 7.9%, suggesting that larger shared backbone can benefit both capabilities. When comparing with the single-task baselines, HIUNI-Dense-4B achieves comparable understanding performance to HIUNI-Und-4B (65.04 vs. 64.58), suggesting that incorporating image generation does not substantially compromise understanding. Notably, MMBench remains comparable, while OCRBench shows only modest decrease, which suggest that the performance gaps relative to the pretrained VLM cannot be solely attributed to joint modeling and may also be influenced by the training data distribution. sections.title: 4.4 ANALYSIS OF RESIDUAL VISUAL PATHWAY
sections.content: Residual Feature Source. The shared ViT and patch merger provide common semantic representation for understanding and generation, but they also reduce fine-grained spatial information before the diffusion head. We therefore examine which feature source is more suitable for the residual pathway used in HIUNI. Specifically, we compare three configurations: directly using pixel-level features before patch embedding (Pixel Features), injecting features from the ViT (ViT Features), or even removing the residual pathway (No Gate). All other architectural and training settings are kept fixed. As shown in Table 5, both residual sources improve image generation over No Gate. The average OneIG score increases from 0.267 to 0.284 with ViT features and further to 0.314 with pixel-level features. Compared with ViT features, pixel-level features provide an additional gain of 0.030, suggesting that features closer to the pixel space better complement the semantic representation produced by the shared ViT. Meanwhile, the average understanding score remains almost unchanged across the three settings, ranging from 65.04 to 65.17. These results support our choice of directly injecting pixel-level information into the generation pathway of HIUNI. Residual Injection Strength. We further analyze how HIUNI uses the pixel-level residual pathway during image generation. Figure 5 visualizes the learned gate strength over diffusion timesteps and training checkpoints. For each timestep, we compute the maximum gate magnitude and normalize it by the global maximum over all plotted timesteps and checkpoints. The gate remains weak at high noise levels and gradually becomes stronger as the input approaches the clean image, suggesting that the residual pathway contributes mainly at later denoising stages where fine-grained spatial details are more important. The overall gate strength also decreases as pretraining progresses, and early checkpoints rely more on the residual pathway. Combined with the residual feature source analysis above, these results suggest that HIUNI can retain semantic modeling in the shared backbone while supplying generation-specific spatial details near the output stage.

sections.title: 4.5 CROSS-TASK INTERACTION
sections.content: Beyond architectural sharing, we further examine whether supervision from one visual task affects the others under the shared backbone. We chose image editing, as it requires both visual understanding and generation capabilities. For fair comparison, we vary the data proportion under fixed training token budget. Specifically, introducing image editing supervision improves the average understanding score from 62.64 to 64.49, while the OneIG average score decreases slightly from 0.538 to 0.528. These results suggest that cross-task transfer and interference can coexist within shared backbone, highlighting both the potential and challenges of joint optimization in highly shared UMMs. Detailed results are provided in Appendix E.

sections.title: 4.6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: The above findings motivate us to reflect on the broader goals of unified multimodal modeling. We discuss three perspectives on its current challenges and future opportunities. From coexistence to synergy. We believe multimodal unification can be viewed at three levels. Capability unification supports both tasks in one model. Collaborative unification allows understanding, reasoning, and generation to work together. Synergistic unification seeks mutual improvement through shared knowledge and supervision. HIUNI mainly explores the first level, while CoT image generation in Appendix takes an initial step toward the second. The editing experiments in Section 4.5 show potential cross-task benefits, but consistent synergy remains an open challenge. Toward stronger cross-task transfer. Beyond better training recipes, data and representation alignment may play more important role in positive transfer, particularly for fine-grained visual capabilities. Recent studies on reconstruction alignment (Xie et al., 2026a), multi-representation generation (Su et al., 2026), and capability transfer (Kang et al., 2026) support this direction. Structured data representations, such as XML-style captions or even image-related code, may connect semantic understanding and visual generation more directly than conventional descriptions. Native unification and agentic systems. Agentic systems can manage long-term memory, planning, and tool use without native interleaved generation. Native UMMs, however, may better support closely coupled understanding, reasoning, and generation within shared context. We see these approaches as complementary, with agents handling long-term coordination and UMMs supporting close multimodal interactions. Whether native interaction offers advantages over modular systems remains an important open question.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present HIUNI, unified multimodal model that harmonizes visual understanding and generation within shared visual space. HIUNI reuses the language aligned ViT and dense Transformer of pretrained VLM for shared semantic modeling, while supplying generation specific spatial details only near the output stage. Experiments show that strong understanding and generation can coexist within such highly shared architecture, without requiring separate visual encoders or task specific backbones. Beyond HIUNI itself, we believe this simple and scalable design provides promising path to extend mature VLMs into more unified models with richer generative capabilities, broader tasks, and more interactive multimodal scenarios.

sections.title: A TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: This section provides additional training details of HIUNI. Following the three-stage procedure described in Section 4.1, training consists of generation warmup, joint pretraining, and supervised fine tuning. The complete training configuration is summarized in Table 6. A.1 TRAINING STAGES During generation warmup, we train the Pixel Diffusion Head and HiGate for 30K steps while keeping the pretrained visual encoder and backbone frozen. Only image generation data are used in this stage, with fixed resolution of 2562. We then unfreeze the full model and perform joint pretraining for 310K steps on pure text modeling, image understanding, and image generation. The generation resolution is progressively increased from 2562 to 20482, while the task sampling ratio remains 0.10:0.30:0.60 throughout pretraining. Finally, supervised fine tuning is performed for 22K steps. Image editing is introduced at this stage while the existing tasks are retained. The task mixture is adjusted between the two fine tuning phases as shown in Table 6. Other phase specific settings, including batch size, learning rate schedule, and image resolution, are also provided in the table. A.2 PIXEL DIFFUSION HEAD CONFIGURATION The Pixel Diffusion Head contains ten Transformer blocks with hidden dimension of 2560, matching the hidden dimension of the shared backbone. For each target visual token, the corresponding 32 32 RGB pixel patch is flattened and projected to the diffusion hidden dimension before being injected through HiGate. The gate is predicted by two layer MLP with SiLU activation. We do not apply an additional sigmoid or tanh activation to the gate output.

sections.content: A.3 OPTIMIZATION AND DIFFUSION SETTINGS We use AdamW throughout training with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, and ϵ = 108. For image editing, the reference and target images share the sequence budget with textual and special tokens, and their resolutions are adjusted jointly to keep the complete sequence within 8192 tokens. The relative loss weight between language modeling and diffusion is set to 0.1:1, except for warmup. For diffusion training, timesteps are sampled from logit normal distribution with µ = 0.8 and σ = 0.8. We use resolution dependent noise scale according to the number of spatial tokens Ng. Specifically, we sample (0, I) and define ϵNg = σNg z, σNg = σ0 (cid:114) Ng , where σ0 = 1, N0 = 64, and σNg is clipped to [1, 8]. The noisy input and target velocity are xt = tx0 + (1 t)ϵNg , = x0 ϵNg . Since the diffusion head directly predicts the clean image ˆx0, we convert it to the velocity prediction used by the training objective as ˆv = ˆx0 xt max(1 t, 0.05) . The denominator is clipped only for numerical stability when approaches one and does not modify the forward interpolation or the target velocity. A.5 TRAINING DATASET Figure 3 summarizes the composition of the training corpus used for image understanding, generation, and editing. For image understanding, the data are mainly distributed across OCR and visual grounding, together with smaller portions of document, arts, sciences and agent-related data. For image generation, the corpus is organized into three major groups, namely nature, people, and design. For image editing, the data mainly cover subject-level, attribute-level, and structure-level edits. The image understanding and generation corpora are constructed from proprietary datasets. For image generation, most training data consist of real image-text pairs, with small amount of synthesized images to control the style. For image understanding, we include training splits from some

Half of the pretraining data contain generated captions, mainly from Qwen series models, while 97% of the SFT samples contain model-generated reasoning traces. For image editing, the corpus contains about 4M examples collected from public datasets and prior work (Ye et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a;c; Wu et al., 2025c; Hu et al., 2024), together with additional private editing pairs produced by our internal data-generation pipeline. For ImgEdit, only the official training split is included in the training corpus, while evaluation is conducted exclusively on its official test split.

sections.content: We evaluate HIUNI on the image understanding benchmarks reported in Table 1. We follow the official benchmark splits and scoring protocols, with benchmark specific answer extraction when required. For the standard image understanding benchmarks, we use min pixels = 262144, max pixels = 4194304, and max model len = 16384. For evaluations with reasoning mode, the model first generates its reasoning process and then produces the final answer. Only the final answer is passed to the benchmark scorer. If valid answer is not completed in the first generation, decoding is continued from the existing context without restarting the example. We follow the official benchmark splits and scoring protocols for all reported evaluations. MathVista. We evaluate on the official MathVista-Mini split and follow its standard evaluation protocol and scorer. The reported score is averaged over two complete evaluations. MMBench. We evaluate MMBench-DEV-EN using the official circular evaluation protocol and report the corresponding overall score. RealWorldQA. We evaluate the official RealWorldQA set and report the EM Overall score. MMStar. We evaluate the official MMStar set and report the Overall score across all categories. HallusionBench. We follow the official evaluation protocol and report its Overall score. AI2D. We evaluate on AI2D-Test and use the official EM protocol for multiple choice prediction. OCRBench. We evaluate OCRBench v1 and report the official Final Score as percentage. OmniDocBench. We evaluate the English split of OmniDocBench v1.0 and report the official OverallEdit score, where lower value indicates better performance. B.

sections.title: IMAGE EDITING
sections.content: We evaluate HIUNI on ImgEdit and GEdit using the same image editing inference pipeline. For both benchmarks, we generate one image for each instruction using 50 sampling steps with the Euler scheduler, shift of 3.0, and CFG scale of 4.0. No additional post processing is applied. ImgEdit. We follow the official evaluation protocol and prompts, using GPT-5.2 as the judge model. Each edited image is scored on 0 to 5 scale, and the Overall score is averaged across edit types. GEdit. We follow the VIEScore evaluation protocol and use GPT-5.2 as the judge model. Each result is evaluated on semantic consistency (G SC) and perceptual quality (G PQ), both on 0 to 10 scale, with their geometric mean reported as O. Scores are first averaged within each edit type and then across all edit types.

sections.title: C OPTIMIZATION STABILITY OF THE PIXEL DIFFUSION HEAD
sections.content: During early development, we observed that the Pixel Diffusion Head with AdaLN frequently produced abrupt loss spikes when trained directly in pixel space. We therefore simplified the diffusion blocks by removing repeated AdaLN modulation while retaining timestep conditioning through the shared backbone and the final prediction layer. Figure 6 shows representative training trajectories. These two runs use different resolution schedules and come from different development stages. The curve without AdaLN exhibits noticeably smoother optimization trajectory with fewer large fluctuations, consistent with the training behavior observed in our subsequent experiments.

Given text prompt p, the model autoregressively generates textual reasoning sequence r, which is then included in the conditioning context as Ccot = (p, r). Image generation follows the same formulation as in Section 3.3, ˆx0 = fθ(xt, t, Ccot) . The reasoning sequence is optimized with the language modeling objective Ltxt, while the target image is optimized with the same diffusion objective Lgen used for standard image generation. Training We obtain the CoT model by continuing training from HIUNI checkpoint after Phase III of joint pretraining, where the training data are derived from UniReason (Wang et al., 2026a). The model is further trained for 10K steps with global batch size of 512. Within the image generation data, standard text-to-image examples and CoT generation examples are sampled with ratio of 1:1, while image understanding and pure-text modeling data are retained during training. No additional backbone or generation module is introduced. Results We evaluate the extension on the WISE benchmark (Niu et al., 2025), with results reported in Table 10. HIUNIw/cot achieves an Overall score of 0.75, exceeding DeepGen 1.0 and Bagel with CoT and remaining competitive with stronger recent image generation models. It performs particularly well on Cultural, Time, and Chemistry, with scores of 0.81, 0.68, and 0.78, respectively. These results are obtained through short fine-tuning stage without modifying the shared backbone or generation pathway, indicating that the HIUNI architecture can be readily extended to reasoning based image generation. In future work, we plan to integrate this capability into the main training pipeline and further study its interaction with standard image generation.

The underlying understanding and generation data sources remain unchanged. As shown in Table 11, editing supervision improves the average understanding score from 62.64 to 64.49, with gains on four of the six evaluated benchmarks. The improvements are particularly pronounced on AI2D-Test and MMStar, which increase by 6.70 and 4.80 points, respectively, indicating that the transferred supervision may be particularly useful for structured visual reasoning. In contrast, HallusionBench decreases by 4.60 points, while OCRBench changes only slightly. This non-uniform pattern suggests that the benefit of editing supervision is task dependent rather than general improvement across all understanding capabilities. At the same time, the average OneIG score slightly decreases from 0.538 to 0.528. Together with the understanding results, this suggests that editing supervision introduces both positive transfer and mild interference under shared training. It can improve several understanding capabilities, while also changing the optimization balance among tasks rather than uniformly benefiting all of them.
